idiom_name: explicit constructor parameters + one composition root (container optional)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: every collaborator is a constructor parameter typed as the consumer's abstraction; the consumer stores it and never constructs, imports or looks it up itself. One composition root per application — main, bootstrapper, application factory — decides the concrete implementations, applies a lifetime (new per use, shared instance, per request) and passes each dependency to the next constructor down the graph. Add a container only when the graph is too large to wire by hand or when a framework owns object creation; the container then plays the injector role and reads the same bindings, while consumers stay untouched. Setter/property injection is reserved for optional dependencies, and interface injection — a second-class form — is driven by the container rather than the consumer.
code_sketch:
class OrderService:                       # consumer declares its needs
    def __init__(self, repo: OrderRepository, clock: Clock):
        self.repo, self.clock = repo, clock

root = CompositionRoot()                 # the only place that knows concretes
repo  = SqlOrderRepository(root.pool)    # lifetime decided here
clock = SystemClock()
service = OrderService(repo, clock)      # handed in, never created inside
pitfalls: Injecting the container, a provider or a locator handle instead of the collaborator — Service Locator behaviour behind an injection-shaped signature.
A dependency injected as a concrete class instead of an abstraction restores compile-time coupling to the implementation.
Lifetimes not decided anywhere: shared and per-use objects mix randomly and state leaks across requests — especially a scoped dependency captured by a singleton (Captive Dependency).
Constructor over-injection: more than four parameters signals a Single-Responsibility violation; seven or more is an anti-pattern requiring a façade or parameters object.
A binding graph that is never validated at start-up fails at the first use deep inside the call stack instead of at bootstrap.
Registering a transient IDisposable without understanding the container's disposal policy leaks memory or holds resources beyond the request.
Ambient mutable context (e.g. a static HttpContext.Current wrapper) injected as a dependency makes unit tests order-sensitive and reintroduces global state.
Capturing a scoped service (e.g. DbContext, request-specific cache) in a singleton through a captured closure or a nested service that outlasts the request — the Captive Dependency anti-pattern.
Using the container to build objects outside its managed scopes (e.g. inside a controller action) bypasses lifetime policy and can cause scope-leak.
Convention-over-configuration wiring without start-up validation produces implicit dependencies that are invisible in code reviews and break silently on minor version upgrades.
One concrete implementation and no test seam in sight: adding an interface and injection for every class 'just in case' adds indirection with zero benefit.
Bastard Injection: constructor defines default values for dependencies, allowing construction without the container and bypassing test seam control.
Async constructors: DI resolution is synchronous but many real services require async initialization — handle this via async factory methods or IAsyncDisposable, not by making constructors async.
Ambient context providers backed by AsyncLocal<T> that outlive the request boundary when captured by singletons.

Direct Container Call (DCC): application code bypasses DI abstractions and calls the container directly to obtain dependencies, coupling business logic to the container API and making the dependency graph invisible at the call site.

Useless Injection: a dependency is declared and injected but never called inside the consumer — it adds noise, memory overhead and a false impression of coupling; detect via coverage or static analysis.

Intransigent Injection (IIJ): the container supplies a dependency that the consumer does not need at construction time, causing unnecessary workload at resolution and obscuring the actual dependency contract.

Door Injection (ODI): infrastructure or bootstrap code depends on the DI mechanism itself (e.g., requiring IServiceProvider to be passed through call chains), leaking container concerns into layers that should be DI-unaware.

Fat DI Class (FDC): a class consumes an excessive number of dependencies, indicating a violation of the Single-Responsibility Principle; the remedy is domain-level decomposition and façade injections for related dependency groups.

Wrong move: routing every class through a DI framework with annotations, tokens and container-managed lifetimes -> libraries and unit tests can no longer construct objects without the framework and the wiring obscures how data actually flows -> instead pass explicit constructor arguments and wire by hand in one composition root, reserving the container for genuinely dynamic binding sets.

Wrong move: relying on runtime reflection to resolve the whole graph -> missing or ambiguous bindings surface as runtime failures at first use, and reflection is unavailable or costly on AOT, mobile and serverless targets -> instead use compile-time graph generation and validation (Dagger, source-generated providers) so unsatisfiable bindings and cycles are build errors.

Wrong move: publishing reusable libraries whose classes are coupled to a container's attributes, tokens and module system -> every consumer inherits that framework's runtime and cannot reuse the classes without it -> instead keep libraries plain classes taking constructor arguments and confine framework-specific glue to the consuming application's composition root.
